b: The famous one: a Starbucks inside the old Joo Chiat Police Station, a two-storey conservation building with shutters and verandahs. This is the centre of your map.
tip: Grab an upstairs seat by the timber shutters. It is one of the prettiest Starbucks in Singapore.

b: Sister of Chinatown's cult September Coffee, in a minimalist corner shophouse. The drinks are as pretty as the room.
tip: Egg mayo sandwich, beef croffle and the Kinako Matcha.

b: A hole-in-the-wall where coffee gets the cocktail-lab treatment. The menu changes with the seasons and the crowd skews young.
tip: Ask for the seasonal signature. They are alcohol-free and built like cocktails.

b: The brunch heavyweight of Joo Chiat with a dedicated filter-coffee bar. After dark it turns into Drunken Farmer, a natural wine bar.
tip: Sourdough pancakes are a Joo Chiat exclusive. Book ahead on weekends.

b: Thick, photogenic Japanese sandos in a calm shophouse. The Har Cheong (prawn-paste chicken) Sando only exists at this outlet.
tip: Tamago Sando for the classic, Har Cheong Sando for the local twist.

b: Donburi, sando and soba in a big airy space right where Joo Chiat Road meets the Koon Seng shophouses.
tip: Perfect pit stop straight after your Koon Seng Road photos.

b: A matcha and wagashi hideout tucked inside the In Good Company boutique. You would walk right past it, which is the point.
tip: Strawberry daifuku with whisked matcha or hojicha.

b: A weekend-only matcha and hojicha bar where your drink comes with a DIY mini bouquet. Mostly takeaway, very Pinterest.
tip: Weekends only, so plan it into a Saturday stroll.

b: Japanese-style coffee and cakes at the quiet northern end of Joo Chiat Road.
tip: Matcha red bean cake.

b: The homegrown pie brand's first full cafe, in a charming shophouse. Sweet tarts, savoury pizza pies and even dog-friendly bakes.
tip: Open till 10pm, so it works as a dessert stop after dinner.

b: A coffee stand hidden in the back alley behind Autocutt Barbershop, with plastic chairs and Vietnamese-style egg coffee.
tip: Enter via the back lane. Go early because it closes mid-afternoon.

b: A roaster since 2016 teams up with Saga Bakeshop. Standing tables, serious beans, fresh bakes.
Minimalist specialty coffee inside the Grafunkt furniture showroom. Quiet, woody and good for journalling.
tip: Coconut latte and a slice of banana cake.

b: A perfume shop that also pulls espresso. Smell your way through the scents with an Orange Americano in hand.
tip: Strawberry Matcha is on the short drinks menu.

b: Rustic bakery cafe with a communal table inside and pet-friendly seats outside. There is no fixed menu because they bake with the flow.
tip: If the pistachio tart is out, get it.

b: A roomy, oriental-styled cafe inside the pastel-pink Joo Chiat Community Club.
tip: Nitro cold brew, then photos against the pink facade.

b: A minimalist filter-coffee bar bringing new life to retro Katong Shopping Centre. Single-origin beans meet homemade kueh.
A tiny bakehouse for freshly baked shio pan, the Japanese salted butter roll, in flavours like truffle and nori.
tip: Pair with a matcha drink. Seats are limited.

b: A Shanghai coffee brand's first Singapore shop, right beside Starbucks Katong Square. Small room, big bean list.
tip: Try the Geisha if it is on.

b: Wood-and-rattan calm in the old Homeground space, pouring coffee from Myanmar that you will struggle to find elsewhere.
The former C Café, reborn with booth seats and moody lighting. A grown-up brunch spot.
tip: Lobster roll.

b: Pastel colour-blocked cafe from the Craftsmen coffee family with a long drinks list, from smoothies to cocktails.
Singapore's bagel legends, canteen-style, with Joo Chiat-only Bagelwiches and St. Ali coffee from Melbourne.
Formerly Wooly's Bagels: a Muslim-owned bagel counter stacking big, loud sandwiches. Takeaway only.

s: Coffee by day · oysters by night
b: A coffee joint with a secret identity. By day it is brunch and mentaiko carbonara. From 5pm it becomes Joo Chiat Oyster House with oysters and cocktails.
Sourdough and brunch inside the Red House, the 1925 bakery building every Katong kid knows.
tip: Scrambled eggs on sourdough.

b: A kopitiam with nearly a century of history, mosaic floors and marble tables. Kaya toast on charcoal-toasted buns, cream horns and kopi.
tip: Go before 10am on weekends. The terrace is pet-friendly.

b: Tropical-French all-day dining in a Peranakan shophouse. Eggs benedict in the morning, steak tartare and wine by night.
The cupcake brand's shophouse outlet with a skylit backyard. Bakes up front, brunch and handmade pasta out back.
Green tiles and timber frames from the team behind Atlas, Apollo, Columbus and Lunar. A modern take on the old-school cafeteria.
All-day French breakfast at Katong V.
A neighbourhood artisan bakery cafe for croissants and loaves, upstairs at Katong V.
Açaí bowls for the post-Pilates glow. It is conveniently in the same building as The Moving Body.
All-day cafe on Tanjong Katong Road that opens early and closes late, which is handy when everything else has shut.
The Atlas Coffeehouse team's east-side brunch spot. Hearty plates, good coffee, pets welcome.
A Melbourne-inspired cafe spread over two shophouse units.
A well-loved bakery that grew out of Hamilton Road. Laminated pastries worth the detour.
Brunch in a leafy former school compound that now houses art studios. Bright, breezy and a little hidden.
tip: Burrata and tomato tartine. Pair it with pottery painting at Hue Your Days next door.

b: An Aussie grocer with an always-busy alfresco bistro. Shop the pretty produce, then stay for brunch.
A collab between The Narrative Coffee and the bakers at Pelle.
A 12-seater run by two friends, serving loaded toasts with no GST and no service charge.
tip: Kayalicious toast or Avo & Eggs.

b: Grilled-sandwich specialists next door to Beastly Girls.
tip: Grilled cheese.

b: A gluten-free bakery cafe started by two Australians. Wholesome and properly tasty.
Traditional Chinese desserts done properly.
tip: Black sesame paste with mini tang yuan, or mango sago.

b: Specialty coffee in a low-key corner of Guillemard, good for a quiet laptop hour.
Crate-dig for records, then stay for pizza. One of the coolest rooms on the street.
A literal hole-in-the-wall with a bright yellow front in the alley beside the Koon Seng shophouses. The brand comes from Bangkok.
tip: Iced Coco Hoji, which is coconut water with hojicha.

n: Joo Chiat Banh Mi Ca Phe
b: A colourful no-pork, no-lard Vietnamese cafe. Baguettes, pho and drip coffee at walkway tables.
A takeaway coffee window run out of a house by Paulin, who is in her seventies. Coffee starts at S$3.
tip: Bring cash and say hi.

b: Frankel Avenue's dependable roaster-cafe for filter coffee and pastries.
A cosy Siglap cafe that also sells flowers.
A big, lofty roastery cafe in Siglap with brunch plates and craft beer.
A Muslim-owned Siglap cafe with Maghreb touches.
tip: Baghrir pancakes or the brioche French toast.

b: A Siglap hidden gem where every dog gets a homemade treat and a water bowl.
Sourdough pizzas and brunch a few steps from the sand. The decor is an extension of the palm trees outside.
Truffle fries with a sea breeze. The glasshouse PS.Cafe sits in the park, so you can cycle right up to it.
A leafy PLQ hangout that runs from lunch to late.
A cute cat-themed cafe at PLQ Plaza that stays open late.
A calm, plant-filled coffee bar next to Paya Lebar MRT.
All-day breakfast plates at the Siglap end of East Coast Road.
A long-running halal cafe born from a love of London coffee houses.
tip: Penny Mac and Cheese.

b: One of Singapore's most-loved bakeries, back after a hiatus. Takeaway only, and everything sells out fast.
tip: Queue before opening. Croissants go first.

b: A roomy new bakery cafe with a counter full of sweet and savoury pastries.
tip: Chocolate almond croissant, then an éclair.

b: A slice of France beside the Koon Seng shophouses. The entrance is on Koon Seng Road.
tip: Hazelnut praline or pistachio tart.

b: Where the botanical gelato phenomenon started. You will smell the thyme-infused cones from down the street.
tip: Strawberry basil or white chrysanthemum in a thyme cone. Pandan is the taste of home.

b: A dark, moody gelato counter with just six flavours, plated like theatre.
tip: Kaya Butter Toast gelato. Open Friday to Sunday only.

b: A spacious deep-red gelato boutique, finally a proper sit-down scoop shop on Joo Chiat Road.
tip: Pistachio on a waffle.

b: Gelato infused with actual hay, served in a narrow shophouse with seats at the back.
tip: Roasted Pistachio or Roasted Cacao with a waffle.

b: A neighbourhood scoop shop on the quieter north stretch of Joo Chiat Road.
An upstairs Chinese dessert parlour for late sweet cravings.
The original banana pie, baked in a basement since 1992. Auntie Peng next door at #B1-92 is the friendly rival.
tip: Buy a slice from each and pick a side.

b: A hole-in-the-wall for old-world European sourdough made with no commercial yeast and no white sugar.
The flagship of Singapore's chocolate cake legends, with a full cafe menu and late hours.
tip: Come after dinner for cake.

b: A vegetarian bakehouse with plant-based cakes.
tip: Mochi donut.

b: A neat little Japanese bakery for soft breads and buns.
A dessert bar that stays open till 2am on weekends, for when the night is not over.
A long-time Tanjong Katong counter for flaky Portuguese egg tarts.
A French-run bakery cafe on Tanjong Katong Road for viennoiserie and quiche.
A cosy old-school bakery cafe for slow catch-ups.
The laksa that beat Gordon Ramsay in a cook-off. The noodles are cut short so you eat the whole bowl with just a spoon.
tip: Add otah on the side.

b: Claimed as the original Katong laksa, served since the 1950s. Creamy, coconut-rich and still argued about.
tip: Do a taste test against 328 across the road.

b: Singapore's oldest Peranakan restaurant. Come for ayam buah keluak and a taste of Nyonya home cooking.
Nyonya rice dumplings and rainbow kueh downstairs, a kebaya and beadwork boutique upstairs. Katong in one shop.
tip: Nyonya chang and kueh lapis. Peek at the kebayas after.

b: A long-running Nyonya restaurant for family-style Peranakan dinners.
Peranakan-leaning plates inside the former Joo Chiat Police Station, next door to the Starbucks.
tip: Beef cheek rendang.

b: Kampong chicken rice that easties will defend forever.

n: Katong Mei Wei Boneless Chicken Rice
b: The queue in the basement says it all. Silky chicken with free-flow achar and soup.

n: Mr and Mrs Mohgan's Super Crispy Roti Prata
b: Regularly named among the crispiest prata in Singapore. It sells out by late morning.
tip: Go early. It is a short walk from the Koon Seng shophouses.

n: Sin Heng Claypot Bak Koot Teh
b: Claypot bak kut teh that has fed Joo Chiat for decades.

n: Kway Guan Huat Joo Chiat Popiah
b: A family business making popiah skins by hand since 1938. Watch the dough being swirled on the hot plate.
One of Singapore's most popular Vietnamese restaurants: loud, fast and always full.
tip: Bun thit nuong cha gio, a dry noodle bowl with grilled pork and spring rolls.

b: Contemporary Southeast Asian plates without the fine-dining stiffness, with local craft beer and natural wine.
An eight-seat counter that tours Southeast Asia through a menu that changes every three months.
A special-occasion Japanese counter. The tallow-aged A5 wagyu is the showstopper.
The Cicheti team's breezy second home, in a corner shophouse. Starters, pastas and pizzas made for sharing.
A neighbourhood tapas bar that feels like a night out in Spain.
Open-fire Italian cooking in a cosy room: octopus, scallops and chops straight off the grill.
A casual spot devoted to handmade Malaysian-style bee hoon, with bowls under ten dollars.
tip: Cheeky Bee Hoon Dry.

b: Behind a door that looks abandoned sits some of the best pizza in Singapore.
tip: Book well ahead.

b: A casual family-run Thai restaurant that regulars call their east-side go-to.
tip: Green curry chicken and claypot vermicelli with prawns.

b: A semi-casual Spanish grill house. The big cuts are built for groups of three or four.
Old-school charcoal steamboat with one house broth, so no one has to argue.
tip: Pork dumplings and fish kuey tiao.

b: Casual Thai at Katong Square.
tip: Red tom yum seafood and pineapple fried rice.

b: Modern Indonesian plates and cocktails in a handsome shophouse.
A retro Japanese grill house with solo-friendly counter seats, each with its own grill. More than 30 cuts.
Looks like a gastropub, cooks like a proper North Indian kitchen.
tip: Chicken dum biryani.

b: One of the first taco joints on the strip, with a wall of hot sauces to test your limits.
American barbecue opened by Americans in 2009, with meats from custom-built smokers.
tip: Baby back ribs. It gets messy.

b: A kopitiam with a craft-beer habit. Stalls range from hokkien mee to burgers.
tip: Yong Huat's hokkien mee is the stall to find.

b: Handmade dim sum and Geylang-style beef hor fun.
A supper institution. Build your own plate of nasi lemak with crispy wings.
KL-style nasi lemak that drew queues from day one. The sambal uses 18 ingredients and cooks for five hours.
The popular Golden Mile wanton mee stall's Joo Chiat home.
Handmade Teochew soon kueh from a tiny neighbourhood shop.
A family-style Italian restaurant that has been wood-firing pizzas in the east for decades.
Peranakan dishes on level four of Village Hotel Katong.
A neighbourhood steakhouse opposite i12 Katong.
A breezy beachfront restaurant inspired by Puglia. Handmade pasta, focaccia and sunsets over the water.
tip: Book a late-afternoon table and stay through golden hour.

b: Where the Jumbo chilli-crab story began in 1987, with tables facing the sea.
A halal spot at Marine Cove famous for buffalo wings.
Singapore's only hawker centre on the beach. Satay smoke, BBQ stingray and sugar cane juice with your toes nearly in the sand.
tip: Come hungry at sunset. Satay, stingray and Haron's satay bee hoon.

b: A small two-storey hawker centre on the edge of Joo Chiat, loved for wanton mee and rojak.
Home of the famous Haig Road Putu Piring, steamed rice cakes filled with gula melaka.
tip: Putu piring, eaten hot.

b: The heart of Malay Singapore. A wet market downstairs, nasi padang, mee rebus and goreng pisang upstairs.
One of Singapore's great hawker centres, with more than a hundred stalls and several famous queues.
tip: Hokkien mee, lor mee and soya beancurd.

n: Marine Parade Central Market & Food Centre
b: The heartland hawker centre beside Parkway Parade and Marine Parade MRT.
When Common Man Coffee Roasters closes for the day, this natural wine bar takes over the room.
Kings Cart's night-time alter ego: oysters, cocktails and a boozy riff on a Solero ice cream.
A no-frills neighbourhood bar with ciders and beers on tap.
Walk to the back of A Vintage Tale and find the pink corner. There is a bar behind it.
A well-known local pie brand with a counter on level one of Roxy Square.
